t: LeetCode 1811 - Find Interview Candidates: Streaks of Medals and Triple Gold
o: Each Contests row names the three medalists of one contest, and consecutive contests are guaranteed to have consecutive IDs. A user qualifies by either winning any medal in three or more consecutive contests, or collecting gold in three different contests anywhere in history. In the example, Sarah qualifies through three golds (190, 193, 196), while Bob (190-192), Alice (191-193) and Quarz (190-194) qualify through streaks; Hercy never appears and is excluded. The consecutive-ID guarantee is the key simplification: three contests in a row are exactly IDs k, k+1, k+2, so no date arithmetic is needed. Any medal means matching against all three medal columns.
k: Consecutive contest IDs turn a streak into an equality pattern: join IDs k, k+1, k+2.
Any medal means the predicate user_id IN (gold_medal, silver_medal, bronze_medal).
UNION deduplicates users who qualify under both rules; UNION-style dedup also matters when melting medal columns.

a.n: Approach 1: Triple Self-Join Plus Grouped Gold Count
a.i: Join three copies of Contests whose IDs line up as k, k+1, k+2 and require the same user to hold some medal in each copy; that certifies a 3-streak. Independently, group gold_medal values to find users with at least three golds, and UNION the two candidate sets with Users to produce name and mail.
s: Self-join Contests c1, c2, c3 with c2.contest_id = c1.contest_id + 1 and c3.contest_id = c1.contest_id + 2
Require u.user_id IN (medals of c1), same for c2 and c3
Separately select gold_medal groups HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
UNION both queries joined back to Users

c.python:
# Database problem - the accepted submission is a single MySQL query:
SELECT u.name, u.mail
FROM Users u
JOIN Contests c1 ON u.user_id IN (c1.gold_medal, c1.silver_medal, c1.bronze_medal)
JOIN Contests c2 ON c2.contest_id = c1.contest_id + 1
                AND u.user_id IN (c2.gold_medal, c2.silver_medal, c2.bronze_medal)
JOIN Contests c3 ON c3.contest_id = c1.contest_id + 2
                AND u.user_id IN (c3.gold_medal, c3.silver_medal, c3.bronze_medal)
UNION
SELECT name, mail
FROM Users
WHERE user_id IN (
    SELECT gold_medal
    FROM Contests
    GROUP BY gold_medal
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
);

a.t: O(M^3) worst case for the triple join where M is the number of contests - fine for small tables but it does not scale.
a.sp: O(Q) for the qualifying intermediate rows before UNION.

a.i: Melt the three medal columns into (contest_id, user_id) rows using UNION, which also deduplicates a user who took two medals in the same contest - crucial so streak counting stays honest. Number each user rows ordered by contest ID; within a user, contest_id - row_number is constant precisely over runs of consecutive contests. Grouping by that value and keeping groups of size >= 3 finds every streak, and this generalizes to n consecutive contests by changing one threshold.
s: Build medals = UNION of (contest, gold), (contest, silver), (contest, bronze)
Add ROW_NUMBER() per user ordered by contest_id
Compute island key contest_id - rn and group by (user_id, island) HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
OR-match users against the gold-count subquery and return name, mail

c.python:
# Database problem - the accepted submission is a single MySQL query:
WITH medals AS (
    SELECT contest_id, gold_medal AS user_id FROM Contests
    UNION
    SELECT contest_id, silver_medal FROM Contests
    UNION
    SELECT contest_id, bronze_medal FROM Contests
),
numbered AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           contest_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY contest_id) AS rn
    FROM medals
),
streaks AS (
    SELECT user_id, contest_id - rn AS grp
    FROM numbered
)
SELECT u.name, u.mail
FROM Users u
WHERE u.user_id IN (
          SELECT user_id
          FROM streaks
          GROUP BY user_id, grp
          HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
      )
   OR u.user_id IN (
          SELECT gold_medal
          FROM Contests
          GROUP BY gold_medal
          HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
      );

a.t: O(M log M) - the window function sorts the melted medal rows once.
a.sp: O(M) for the melted and numbered intermediate relations.

w: Lead with the self-join if the interviewer wants something quick and correct, then offer gaps-and-islands as the scalable generalization - it directly answers the stated follow-ups: for n consecutive contests just change the HAVING threshold, and restricting to contests the user registered for is one extra inner join before the window computation. Pitfalls: using UNION ALL when melting columns (duplicate medal rows from the same contest corrupt streaks), forgetting DISTINCT-free semantics of UNION, and testing only gold in the streak condition.
